title: Executive Summary
text:
Executive Summary
The Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) Civil Services Examination (CSE) is a single national
examination that fills roughly two dozen senior government posts, including the Indian Administrative Service
(IAS), the Indian Police Service (IPS) and the Indian Foreign Service (IFS). It is conducted in three
successive stages: the Preliminary Examination (objective), the Main Examination (written, descriptive) and
the Personality Test (interview). Prelims is a screening test only; only Main Examination marks and interview
marks decide the final rank.

The examination is genuinely competitive but the raw odds are widely misread. In the CSE 2025 cycle,
9,37,876 candidates applied, 5,76,793 actually appeared in Prelims, 14,161 qualified for Mains, 2,736
reached the interview, and 958 were finally recommended. That is about 1 selection per 602 candidates who
sat Prelims - not per applicant. Roughly two out of five candidates who apply never write the exam at all.

This handbook exists so that a first-time aspirant can decide, on evidence rather than rumour, whether to
commit to UPSC, and if so how. It covers eligibility and attempts, the full examination process, the pattern
and marking system, the syllabus in plain language, the real competition level, optional-subject selection, a
stage-wise booklist, preparation timelines from 12 to 24 months, study systems, current affairs, answer
writing, coaching economics, cost planning, common mistakes, stress and backup careers, and a day-by-day
plan for the first 30 days.

  What this handbook is not: it is not a promise of selection, and no book, coaching course or timetable can
  guarantee a result. No number of hours, books or attempts guarantees success.
  Three facts worth carrying through every page: (1) read the official syllabus before buying anything; (2) Prelims
  and Mains are different skills and must be trained separately; (3) the decision of whether to prepare at all is as
  important as how to prepare.

 Stage                     Nature                         Marks that count       Purpose

 Preliminary               Objective, 2 papers            None for final merit   Screening to Mains only

 Main (written)            9 descriptive papers           1,750 of 2,025         Merit for interview call

 Personality Test          Interview                      275 of 2,025           Final merit and service fit
Source: UPSC CSE 2026 Notification (Notice No. 05/2026-CSE, 4 Feb 2026).
keyTakeaways: Prelims is a screening stage; its marks do not add to final merit.
Read the current official notification before acting on eligibility or application rules.
The handbook treats planning advice and estimates differently from official facts.
nextAction: Use the “Start here” checklist and open the official CSE notification.
source: UPSC CSE Complete Beginner’s Handbook, research cutoff 12 October 2026

title: Understanding UPSC and the Civil Services
text:
What UPSC is, and what it does
The Union Public Service Commission is a constitutional body created under Article 315 of the Constitution of
India. Its job is to recruit people to the higher civil services of the Union and to advise the government on
recruitment matters. It does not govern; it selects. For the Civil Services Examination, UPSC conducts the
examination, but the rules - who is eligible, how many vacancies, how reservation applies - are framed by the
Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) and published in the Gazette of India.

That division matters to a beginner: when rules change, the change comes from DoPT and appears in the
annual notification. UPSC's own website (upsc.gov.in) publishes the notification, the syllabus, the calendar,
question papers, results and cut-offs.

UPSC, IAS, IPS, IFS and IRS are not the same thing
The most common beginner confusion is treating 'UPSC', 'IAS' and 'civil services' as synonyms. They are not.
•
     UPSC is the commission that conducts many examinations - Civil Services, Indian Forest Service,
     Engineering Services, Combined Defence Services, and more.
•
     The Civil Services Examination (CSE) is the one examination most people mean when they say 'UPSC'. It
     recruits to about two dozen services at once.
•
     IAS, IPS and IFS are individual services. IAS and IPS are All India Services; IFS is a Central Service. You
     do not choose to 'sit the IAS exam' - you sit the CSE and, if you rank high enough, you may be allotted the
     IAS.

There is no separate 'IAS examination'. The phrase is shorthand for the Civil Services Examination, whose
top ranks are usually allotted the IAS. The only major service with a genuinely separate examination is the
Indian Forest Service (IFoS): candidates write the Civil Services Preliminary paper as a screen, then a
separate IFoS Main examination.

What you are actually competing for: the service list
The CSE fills three tiers of posts. All India Services (IAS, IPS) are constituted under Article 312; officers are
allotted a state cadre and serve both state and Union through their careers. Central Civil Services, Group A
serve the Union in a specific department - diplomacy, tax, audit, railways, defence accounts. Group B
services are Union Territory and secretariat services, with entry grades a step below Group A.

    Tier                            Examples                                           Where officers serve

    All India Services              IAS, IPS                                           State cadre plus Union deputation

    Central Group A                 IFS, IRS (Income Tax), IRS (Customs &              A specific Union ministry or department
                                    Indirect Taxes), IA&AS;, ICAS, IDAS, IDES,
                                    IPoS, IRMS, IIS, ITS, ICLS

    Central Group B                 AFHQCS, DANICS, DANIPS, PONDICS,                   Union Territories and secretariat grades
                                    PONDIPS
Source: Service tiers per DoPT CSE Rules and the UPSC CSE 2026 notification service list.

The list has been rationalised in recent years. The old Railway Traffic, Personnel and Accounts services were
merged into the Indian Railway Management Service (IRMS), and some services such as the Indian
Ordnance Factories Service no longer appear. Online lists copied from before 2019 are often outdated.

Clearing UPSC does not guarantee the IAS
This single misunderstanding causes the most disappointment. Selection to the CSE earns you a place in the
merit list and a service - not necessarily the service you wanted. Which service you get depends on your
rank, your category, the number and category-wise distribution of vacancies that year, the service
preferences you record in the Detailed Application Form (DAF), and medical fitness for services with physical
standards. A candidate ranked in the 900s will not receive the IAS, whose intake is a fraction of total
vacancies.

    Service                      2025 vacancies        Broad function                                   Work environment

    IAS                          180                   District administration, state secretariat,      Field postings, then
                                                       policy                                           secretariat and deputation

    IPS                          150                   Law and order, internal security,                Field police postings,
                                                       intelligence                                     physical standards apply

    IFS                          55                    Diplomacy, embassies and consulates              Ministry of External Affairs
                                                       abroad                                           and missions abroad

    Central Gr. A                507                   Tax, audit, accounts, railways, defence,         Mostly departmental,
                                                       communication                                    largely office-based

    Central Gr. B                195                   UT administration and secretariat grades         Union Territory
                                                                                                        administrations
Source: Vacancy figures: UPSC/PIB final-result press note for CSE 2025 (6 March 2026). Figures are for one cycle and change every year.

Training: what LBSNAA and other academies involve
After allocation, officers undergo a probationary training period at a service academy. IAS officers train at the
Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration (LBSNAA) in Mussoorie; IPS officers at the Sardar
Vallabhbhai Patel National Police Academy in Hyderabad; IFS officers at the Foreign Service Institute.
Training combines academic coursework, field attachments, language study, physical training and, for the
IAS, the district-training and Bharat Darshan components. It is demanding and is graded; probation can, in
principle, be extended.

Twelve misconceptions worth discarding now
•
     That clearing the exam means the IAS - it does not (see above).
•
     That the salary makes you rich - pay is set by the 7th Pay Commission scales, comfortable but not
     extraordinary; the draw is authority and responsibility, not wealth.
•
     That officers have unlimited power - every decision sits inside rules, courts, auditors and seniority.
•
     That work-life balance is always poor - it varies sharply by service, posting and phase of career; field
     postings in the IAS and IPS are heavier than departmental desk roles.
•
     That transfers are rare - transfers are routine, especially in the IAS and IPS, and cadres determine where
     you serve.
•
     That the job is unlosable - it is secure, but discipline and conduct rules are real.
•
     That coaching is mandatory - lakhs succeed without full coaching, and many with coaching do not.
•
     That the exam is only about memorising facts - the Mains rewards analysis and structured argument far
     more than recall.
•
     That a high mark in school or a good degree predicts selection - it helps but does not decide.
•
     That English fluency decides the interview - content and clarity matter more than accent.
•
     That one attempt can be casually spent - each appearance is consumed permanently.
•
     That UPSC is the only respectable career - it is one option among many good ones.
keyTakeaways: UPSC is the recruiting commission; CSE is an examination, not a service.
Clearing CSE does not guarantee IAS; rank, preferences, vacancies and eligibility affect allocation.
Service roles differ substantially in work setting and responsibilities.
nextAction: Write down the work and services you are genuinely aiming for, beyond status.
source: UPSC CSE Complete Beginner’s Handbook, research cutoff 12 October 2026

title: Should You Prepare for UPSC?
text:
This part is deliberately blunt. The examination is long, uncertain and costly in time. Deciding to prepare is a
life decision, and it deserves an honest audit before money and years are committed.

The dimensions that actually matter
•
        Academic base - a graduate degree is required. A background in humanities or general reading helps, but
        engineering, medicine, commerce and science graduates top the exam every year; the CSE 2025 topper
        is an MBBS graduate.
•
        Interest in governance and the world - sustained curiosity about polity, economy, history, geography and
        current affairs predicts endurance better than any aptitude test.
•
        Reading ability - you must read dense non-fiction quickly and retain the argument, not just the facts.
•
        Writing ability - the Mains and interview reward clear, structured, analytical writing under time pressure.
•
        Consistency and tolerance for uncertainty - months of work with no feedback, then a result that can hinge
        on a few marks.
•
        Financial runway and family responsibility - preparation can take 1-3 years; the opportunity cost is real.
•
        Mental resilience - isolation, comparison and repeated attempts are part of the experience for many.

A self-assessment questionnaire
Score each statement from 0 (not true of me) to 3 (very true). This is a reflection tool, not a scientific predictor
of selection. There is no pass mark; the point is to see your own profile clearly.

    #        Statement                                                                                           Score 0-3

    1        I can read a serious 20-page article and summarise its argument from memory.

    2        I follow national news and can explain why an event matters, not just what happened.

    3        I can sit and study for 2-3 focused hours without checking my phone.

    4        I can write 250 words on a topic with a clear structure in 20 minutes.

    5        I have at least 12 months of financial runway without needing a job.

    6        My family understands this is a long, uncertain process.

    7        I want the work of governance, not only the status of an officer.

    8        I can keep going for months without external validation.

    9        I have a realistic backup plan if selection does not happen.

    10       I am willing to change my method when evidence says it is not working.
Source: Mentor-designed reflection tool; not an official UPSC instrument.

Read your own pattern rather than the total. Low scores on reading and writing are trainable and should not
stop you. Low scores on financial runway, family understanding or resilience are structural and should shape
your model - part-time study, a shorter horizon, or a different path altogether.

Full-time, part-time, or job-plus-preparation
    Model                        Suits                                                Watch out for

    Full-time                    Graduates with 18-24 months of runway and            Losing touch with the job market;
                                 family support                                       monotony and isolation

 Model                    Suits                                            Watch out for

 Job-plus                 Working professionals with a stable,             Fatigue; needs a ruthless weekly schedule
                          bounded-hours job

 Part-time                Students and those who must earn                 Slow coverage; requires longer horizon

  UPSC is not automatically the best option for everyone. It suits people who want the work and can absorb the
  uncertainty. It is a poor fit for anyone who mainly wants a government salary, a title, or a way to postpone a
  career decision.
keyTakeaways: Test career fit and finances before buying courses.
The self-assessment score is reflective, not a validated predictor.
A 30-day pilot can test study routine, reading, PYQs and CSAT.
nextAction: Complete the source’s self-assessment and define a review date.
source: UPSC CSE Complete Beginner’s Handbook, research cutoff 12 October 2026

title: Eligibility, Attempts, Age and Documents
text:
Everything below reflects the CSE 2026 notification (Notice No. 05/2026-CSE dated 4 February 2026) and
the CSE 2026 Rules published by DoPT in the Gazette of India Extraordinary of the same date. Rules repeat
each year, but the reference date and some details move with each notification - always verify against the
notification for your own cycle.

Nationality
•
     For the IAS, IPS and IFS, a candidate must be a citizen of India.
•
     For all other services, a candidate may be a citizen of India, or a subject of Nepal or Bhutan, or a Tibetan
     refugee who came to India before 1 January 1962 intending to settle permanently, or a person of Indian
     origin who migrated from a listed set of countries intending to settle permanently.
•
     Candidates in the non-citizen categories must hold a certificate of eligibility issued by the Government of
     India; they may be admitted to the examination but appointment follows only after the certificate is issued.

Educational qualification
A candidate must hold a graduate degree from a university incorporated by an Act of the central or state
legislature, or established by an Act of Parliament, or declared deemed a university under Section 3 of the
UGC Act, 1956, or possess an equivalent qualification. Final-year students may apply, but must produce
proof of passing (degree certificate, final marksheet or provisional certificate) within the time allowed by the
rules after the result.

Age limit and relaxations
For CSE 2026 a candidate must have attained 21 years and must not have attained 32 years on 1 August
2026 - that is, born between 2 August 1994 and 1 August 2005. The reference date moves with each
notification.

    Category                            Upper age          Relaxation                  Born between (CSE 2026)

    General / EWS                       32                 None                        2 Aug 1994 - 1 Aug 2005

    OBC (NCL)                           35                 +3 years                    2 Aug 1991 - 1 Aug 2005

    SC / ST                             37                 +5 years                    2 Aug 1989 - 1 Aug 2005

    PwBD (benchmark disability)         42                 +10 years                   2 Aug 1984 - 1 Aug 2005

    Ex-servicemen (5+ yrs service)      37                 +5 years                    2 Aug 1989 - 1 Aug 2005

    Defence disabled in operations      35                 +3 years                    2 Aug 1991 - 1 Aug 2005
Source: UPSC CSE 2026 notification, Para 3(II). Minimum age is 21 for every category; there is no lower-age relaxation.

There is no separate age relaxation for EWS candidates - they follow the General limits. SC/ST/OBC
candidates who are also ex-servicemen or PwBD receive both relaxations cumulatively (for example, an OBC
candidate with benchmark disability reaches an upper age of 45). Date of birth is accepted only as recorded
in the matriculation or secondary school leaving certificate.

Attempts: what counts and how many you get
Merely applying does not consume an attempt. Appearing in even one paper of the Preliminary Examination
does. Once you have appeared, the attempt is counted even if your candidature is later cancelled or
disqualified.

    Category                                                                        Maximum attempts

    General / EWS                                                                   6

    OBC (NCL)                                                                       9

    SC / ST                                                                         Unlimited, up to the age limit

    PwBD - General / EWS / OBC                                                      9

    PwBD - SC / ST                                                                  Unlimited, up to the age limit
Source: UPSC CSE 2026 notification, Para 3(IV).

PwBD, government employees and other special cases
•
     Persons with Benchmark Disability (40% or more disability) receive an age relaxation of 10 years, extra
     attempts, fee exemption, compensatory time in objective papers where eligible, and a scribe facility under
     the rules. Appointment still requires meeting the functional requirements and medical standards of the
     service allocated.
•
     Government servants and certain public-sector employees may apply, subject to the conditions in the
     notification and to producing a no-objection certificate where required.
•
     Candidates who have already been appointed to a service after a previous CSE may face restrictions on
     re-appearing; the rules state these conditions explicitly and they should be read in the notification for the
     relevant year.

Medical and physical standards: general eligibility versus service-specific
There are two separate layers. General eligibility - nationality, age, degree, attempts - decides whether you
may sit the examination. Medical fitness decides which service you may be appointed to. A candidate can
clear the examination and still be found unfit for a specific service, in which case the service allocated may
change.

Medical examination is conducted by a Central Standing Medical Board after the Personality Test, for
candidates likely to be recommended. Services with physical standards include the IPS, the Railway
Protection Force and other police services, and technical services. Indicative minimum standards (which
have category and region-specific relaxations) include:

    Standard                               Men                      Women                   Notes

    Height - general minimum               163 cm                   150 cm                  Applies to specified services

    Height - IPS / police services         165 cm                   150 cm                  Relaxations for ST and listed hill and
                                                                                            north-eastern races

    Chest (expanded / expansion)           84 cm / 5 cm             79 cm / 5 cm            For services with chest standards

    Distant vision (corrected)             6/6 better eye, 6/6      Same                    Best correction permitted; squint is a
                                           worse eye                                        disqualification
Source: UPSC/DoPT physical-examination regulations (Appendix-III to the CSE Rules). Indicative only - the current notification and
Appendix-III govern.

Document checklist
Assemble these in advance. Formats, validity periods and cut-off dates must be checked against the
notification for your cycle - do not assume one certificate format works for every recruitment.
•
     Educational documents - degree certificate, final marksheet or provisional certificate; matriculation
     certificate for date of birth.

•
    Date-of-birth proof - matriculation or secondary school leaving certificate.
•
    Category certificate - SC/ST/OBC (Non-Creamy Layer) in the prescribed format, valid on the closing date,
    with the OBC-NCL validity period observed.
•
    EWS certificate - income and asset certificate in the prescribed format for the financial year specified in the
    notification.
•
    PwBD certificate - benchmark-disability certificate in the prescribed format.
•
    Photo identity - Aadhaar, passport, or another listed photo ID for the exam hall.
•
    Photographs - recent passport photographs to the specification in the application.
•
    Other declarations - ex-servicemen, government-servant and similar declarations where applicable.

    An OBC or EWS claim is verified against documents submitted and can be rejected if the certificate is in the
    wrong format or expired. Read the certificate requirements in the notification for your cycle before applying, not
    after.
keyTakeaways: Age, attempts, nationality, degree proof and special-category provisions must be checked against the target-cycle notice.
An attempt ordinarily counts after appearing in a Prelims paper, not merely filling a form.
Certificates have format, validity and deadline requirements.
nextAction: Check every eligibility clause against the latest notification before applying.
source: UPSC CSE Complete Beginner’s Handbook, research cutoff 12 October 2026

title: The Complete Examination Process
text:
The journey from notification to joining has thirteen identifiable steps. Each has a deadline, a document
requirement and a common failure mode.

                               1. Notification and eligibility check (January-February)

                                                            v
                                  2. Online application and One-Time Registration

                                                            v
                                    3. Application correction window (if offered)

                                                            v
                                      4. Admit card and exam-day instructions

                                                            v
                                       5. Preliminary Examination (late May)

                                                            v
                                      6. Prelims result - qualification for Mains

                                                            v
                                    7. Detailed Application Form (DAF) for Mains

                                                            v
                                      8. Main Examination (August, five days)

                                                            v
                                             9. Personality Test / Interview

                                                            v
                                                   10. Final merit list

                                                            v
                                         11. Service and cadre preference

                                                            v
                                      12. Medical examination and verification

                                                            v
                                     13. Service allocation, training and joining

Stage by stage: what to do, what is evaluated
1. Notification and eligibility verification
The notification is published on upsc.gov.in. Download the notification and the syllabus, read the eligibility
paragraphs for your category, and note every deadline. What qualifies you for the next stage here is a
correct, complete application - not marks.

2. Online application and registration
Applications are made through the UPSC online portal (upsconline.gov.in). First-time candidates complete
One-Time Registration (OTR), which stores personal details for future applications. Common errors:
mismatched name or date of birth against documents, wrong category, and failure to upload a compliant
photograph and signature.

3. Application correction
UPSC sometimes offers a correction window after the application closes. Corrections are limited to specified
fields and are not guaranteed every year. Do not rely on the window - apply correctly the first time.

4. Admit card and examination day
The e-admit card is released a week to ten days before the examination. Check the centre and carry the
admit card plus a valid photo ID. Reach the centre well before reporting time; late entry is not permitted.

5-6. Preliminary Examination and its result
Prelims is held on a single day in late May: General Studies Paper I in the forenoon session and CSAT
(Paper II) in the afternoon. Both papers are mandatory - a candidate who does not appear in both is
disqualified. The result, published in mid-June, lists roll numbers of those shortlisted for Mains. In CSE 2026,
13,343 candidates were shortlisted against 1,016 vacancies.

7. Detailed Application Form (DAF) for Mains
Qualified candidates must log in during the prescribed window, pay the Mains fee where applicable, update
scribe and assistive-device details, and fill cadre and service preferences. In CSE 2026 this window ran from
19 to 28 June. Even candidates with nothing to change must log in and submit, or the Mains admit card is not
generated.

8. Main Examination
Mains is nine descriptive papers written over five days in August. Two language papers are qualifying; the
remaining seven carry merit. The evaluation here is depth, structure and analytical writing, not recall.

9. Personality Test
Candidates who clear Mains are called for an interview of 275 marks. It is a personality-assessment
conversation anchored in the DAF, not a current-affairs quiz. About twice the number of vacancies are called
- 2,736 for 958 recommendations in CSE 2025.

10-13. Final list, preferences, medical and joining
The final merit list combines Mains and interview marks. Service and cadre preferences (filled at DAF stage)
are matched against rank and vacancies. Medical examination and document verification follow, then service
allocation, training and joining. Appointment is subject to satisfactory verification of eligibility and reservation
claims.

Qualifying, merit-counting and screening papers
 Type                               Papers                                               Effect

 Screening                          Prelims GS Paper I and CSAT                          Decides who reaches Mains;
                                                                                         marks not carried forward

 Qualifying                         Mains Paper A (Indian language), Paper B (English)   Must be passed; marks not
                                                                                         counted for merit

 Merit-counting                     Essay, GS-I to GS-IV, Optional I and II, and the     Decide the final rank
                                    interview
Source: UPSC CSE 2026 notification, Section II.

Provisional result, final result, recommendation, allocation, appointment
These are different things and are often confused. A provisional result declares qualification subject to
verification. A final result is the merit list. A recommendation means UPSC has placed you on the list sent to
the government. Service allocation is the government assigning a service and cadre. Appointment is the
formal offer after verification and medical clearance. Candidature can be kept provisional even in the final
result - in CSE 2025, 348 recommended candidates were provisional.
keyTakeaways: The process includes notification, application, Prelims, Mains, Personality Test and administrative allocation/appointment steps.
Qualifying, screening and merit-counting are different.
A shortlist or recommendation is not the same as a final service/cadre appointment.
nextAction: Turn each official deadline into a calendar reminder.
source: UPSC CSE Complete Beginner’s Handbook, research cutoff 12 October 2026

title: Complete Exam Pattern and Marking System
text:
A. Preliminary Examination
Prelims has two compulsory objective papers of 200 marks each, of two hours each. Only GS Paper I counts
for shortlisting; CSAT is qualifying at 33% (66 of 200 marks). Both papers are mandatory, and a candidate
who misses either is disqualified.

 Paper                                    Marks              Questions             Marks / question               Negative marking

 GS Paper I                               200                100                   2.0                            1/3 of the marks
                                                                                                                  (0.66)

 CSAT (GS Paper II)                       200                80                    2.5                            1/3 of the marks
                                                                                                                  (0.83)
Source: UPSC CSE 2026 notification and syllabus, Section II(A).

The Prelims cut-off is computed only on GS Paper I, after applying the CSAT qualifying filter. Cut-off marks
are category-wise and change every year with paper difficulty and the candidate pool. In CSE 2025 the
General cut-off was 92.66 out of 200. Because the Prelims is a screen, its marks are not counted in the final
merit list.

Why candidates fail Prelims while knowing many answers
Prelims punishes three errors more than ignorance. First, accuracy: with 1/3 negative marking, a net-positive
strategy matters more than attempting everything. Second, time management: 100 questions in two hours
leaves roughly 72 seconds each, and CSAT's 80 questions demand even tighter control. Third, excessive
guessing: candidates who attempt all 100 questions often score below those who attempt 80 well. Qualifying
CSAT is a different task from scoring high on GS Paper I - CSAT rewards speed and comprehension, GS
Paper I rewards breadth and precision.

B. Main Examination
Mains is nine descriptive papers of three hours each, written over five days. Papers A and B are qualifying;
the rest count for merit. The written total is 1,750 marks.

 Paper           Subject                                                           Marks                 Status

 Paper A         Indian language (one of the Eighth Schedule languages)            300                   Qualifying

 Paper B         English                                                           300                   Qualifying

 Paper I         Essay                                                             250                   Merit

 Paper II        GS-I - Heritage, History, Geography, Society                      250                   Merit

 Paper III       GS-II - Governance, Constitution, Polity, Social Justice, IR      250                   Merit

 Paper IV        GS-III - Technology, Economy, Environment, Security,              250                   Merit
                 Disaster

 Paper V         GS-IV - Ethics, Integrity and Aptitude                            250                   Merit

 Paper VI        Optional subject Paper I                                          250                   Merit

 Paper VII       Optional subject Paper II                                         250                   Merit

 -               Written sub-total                                                 1,750                 Merit

 -               Personality Test                                                  275                   Merit

 -               Grand total                                                       2,025                 Merit
Source: UPSC CSE syllabus, Section II(B). Language papers must be passed but their marks do not count.

The qualifying language papers are set at matriculation standard. Paper A is answered in an Eighth Schedule
language of the candidate's choice; Paper B in English. Failing either paper means the candidate is not
considered, regardless of GS performance. This is rare but real, and it is the reason candidates should never
skip these papers.

C. Personality Test
The interview carries 275 marks. Its purpose is to assess personality, judgement, balance, clarity of thought
and suitability for a career in public service. It is both a personality assessment and, to a limited extent, a
knowledge conversation - but it is not a quiz. Questions are anchored in the Detailed Application Form: home
district, state, graduation subject, work experience, hobbies and interests, and current affairs.
•
    Situational and ethical questions test judgement, not doctrine.
•
    Body language matters only in the ordinary sense of being calm, attentive and honest.
•
    English fluency is not scored as such - clarity of thought is.
•
    Coaching and model answers can make an interview sound rehearsed; authenticity scores better.

    Distinguish the official pattern from coaching folklore. UPSC publishes the marks and qualifying rules; it does
    not publish 'correct' interview answers, and no board expects a particular worldview.
keyTakeaways: Both Prelims papers are compulsory.
GS-I sets the screening cutoff; CSAT is qualifying under the 2026 reference rules.
Prelims marks are excluded from final merit; wrong MCQs incur a penalty.
nextAction: Practise the scoring formula and diagnose CSAT early.
source: UPSC CSE Complete Beginner’s Handbook, research cutoff 12 October 2026

title: The Syllabus Explained in Simple Language
text:
This part paraphrases the official syllabus area by area. It is not a substitute for the official syllabus -
download that from upsc.gov.in and read it first. For each area: what it means, what the examiner expects,
and how to begin.

Prelims - General Studies Paper I
Seven broad areas: current events of national and international importance; history of India and the Indian
national movement; Indian and world geography (physical, social, economic); Indian polity and governance;
economic and social development; environmental ecology, biodiversity and climate change; and general
science. The examiner expects breadth and factual precision, not depth in one area. Begin with NCERT
classes 6-10 for history, geography and polity, and one national newspaper.

Prelims - CSAT (Paper II)
Comprehension; interpersonal and communication skills; logical reasoning and analytical ability;
decision-making and problem-solving; general mental ability; basic numeracy and data interpretation at Class
X level. It is qualifying at 33%, but it must be passed. Begin by diagnosing your speed with a timed mock,
then drill comprehension and data interpretation, which carry the most weight.

Mains - Essay
Two essays chosen from a list of topics, written in 1,000-1,200 words each. The examiner expects a clear
central idea, a coherent structure, illustration, balance and a decisive conclusion. Begin by writing one essay
a week and getting it read.

Mains - General Studies I
Indian heritage and culture; modern Indian history and the freedom struggle; world history from the
eighteenth century; Indian society and diversity; social issues; and geography of India and the world. The
examiner wants cause-and-effect and analysis, not timelines. Connect every static theme to a current
example.

Mains - General Studies II
The Constitution, polity, governance, social justice and international relations. The examiner expects you to
reason about institutions, rights, welfare delivery and India's foreign policy with balance and examples.

Mains - General Studies III
Technology, economic development, biodiversity, environment, security and disaster management. The
examiner expects a working understanding of the economy, government schemes, and India's security and
environmental challenges, used to support arguments.

Mains - General Studies IV (Ethics)
Ethics and human interface; attitude; aptitude and foundational values; emotional intelligence; thinkers and
administrators; public-service values; probity in governance; and case studies. The examiner expects applied
ethical reasoning, not definitions. Practise case studies using stakeholder analysis and practical solutions.

Mains - Optional subject
Two papers at roughly honours-degree level. For engineering, medical science and law, the level
corresponds to the bachelor's degree. Choose one subject from the official list (Part 8 covers how).

title: Understanding the Competition Level
text:
Competition is best read stage by stage, because each stage removes a large share of candidates. The
figures below are official where available and are labelled by cycle and stage.

 Cycle            Applied                         Appeared in Prelims                Qualified Mains                 Recommended

 2025             9,37,876                        5,76,793                           14,161                          958

 2024             9,92,599                        5,83,213                           14,627                          1,009

 2023             Not published                   Not published                      14,624                          1,016

 2022             11,35,697                       5,73,735                           13,090                          933

 2021             10,93,984                       5,08,619                           9,214                           685
Source: UPSC/PIB result press notes; compiled from official statistics. 'Not published' means the figure is not available from an official
source.

In CSE 2025, 13,343 candidates were shortlisted for Mains in the 2026 cycle against 1,016 vacancies -
roughly thirteen times the vacancies, in line with the rule that Mains intake is about twelve to thirteen times
the number of posts. About twice the vacancies are called for interview.

Applicants versus examinees versus qualifiers
Four different ratios are quoted as 'the selection rate', and they differ enormously. Against applicants, CSE
2025 was about 1 in 979. Against those who actually sat Prelims, it was about 1 in 602. Stage by stage, the
picture changes again: about 61% of applicants appeared in Prelims, about 2.5% of those who appeared
qualified for Mains, about 19% of Mains-qualified reached the interview, and about 35% of interview
candidates were recommended. A high applicant count therefore overstates the competition, because
roughly two in five applicants never write the exam.

Category-wise cut-offs, CSE 2025
 Category                                Prelims (of 200)                   Mains (of 1,750)                   Final (of 2,025)

 General                                 92.66                              739                                963

 EWS                                     89.34                              706                                926

 OBC                                     92.00                              717                                931

 SC                                      84.00                              700                                905

 ST                                      82.66                              694                                902

 PwBD-1                                  76.66                              703                                917

 PwBD-2                                  54.66                              708                                944

 PwBD-3                                  40.66                              536                                804

 PwBD-5                                  40.66                              451                                631
Source: UPSC minimum qualifying marks for CSE 2025, released 9 March 2026. Cut-offs change every cycle.

Two lessons sit in this table. First, the gap between the Mains cut-off (739) and the final cut-off (963) for the
General category is 224 marks, against an interview maximum of 275 - the interview is not a formality, it
decides ranks. Second, cut-offs are a moving target: the General Prelims cut-off has ranged from about 75 to
98 over recent years, so a mock score must be judged against the trend, not a single year.

Why the raw applicant number misleads
The examination is hard for structural reasons, not only for its size: the syllabus is broad across many
disciplines; it is conducted in three stages that reward different skills; vacancies are a small fraction of
examinees; negative marking punishes guessing; Mains demands sustained answer-writing practice; the
optional subject is a large separate commitment; and the whole process takes more than a year from
application to result, with no interim reward. None of this is defeated by any fixed number of hours or books -
and no coaching centre's 'success rate' should be read as a personal probability.
keyTakeaways: Applications and actual attendance are different denominators.
Historical cutoffs and candidate counts describe past cycles, not personal probabilities.
Category and stage-specific marks should not be mixed.
nextAction: Record a baseline mock score and compare it only with the correct paper and scale.
source: UPSC CSE Complete Beginner’s Handbook, research cutoff 12 October 2026

title: Choosing the Optional Subject
text:
The optional subject carries 500 of the 1,750 written marks - nearly 29% of the written total and about 25% of
the final 2,025. It is the single largest block a candidate controls, and a poor choice is costly because it is
hard to change after Mains preparation begins.

How to evaluate a subject, not rank it
No subject is universally best. The right method is to score each candidate subject on the dimensions that
matter to you, then test the top two before committing.

 Dimension                                  What to check

 Syllabus fit                               Read the official syllabus and mark topics you can already handle

 Material availability                      Are there reliable standard books and past papers?

 Guidance                                   Is there a teacher or evaluator you can access for feedback?

 Interest and stamina                       Can you study this subject deeply for a year without boredom?

 Overlap                                    How much does it overlap GS and Essay, saving revision time?

 Writing load                               Does it demand diagram-heavy or essay-heavy answers?

 Graduation background                      Does your degree give you a head start?

 Language demands                           Any terminology or script issues for you?

Commonly chosen subjects: honest trade-offs
 Subject                          Advantages                                            Limitations

 Sociology                        Overlaps GS-I and Essay; concise syllabus;            Heavy competition; scoring can be
                                  accessible material                                   unpredictable

 Anthropology                     Structured syllabus; strong overlap with society      Technical vocabulary; needs disciplined
                                  topics                                                writing

 Geography                        Strong overlap with GS-I and GS-III; visual           Mapping-heavy; large factual load
                                  answers

 History                          Overlaps GS-I; familiar to many graduates             Long syllabus; answer-writing demands
                                                                                        precision

 Political Science & IR           Direct overlap with GS-II                             IR portion needs current-affairs depth

 Public Administration            Overlaps GS-II governance themes                      Theoretical; perceived scoring volatility

 Philosophy                       Concise syllabus; strong for Ethics overlap           Abstract; needs careful structuring

 Mathematics                      Objective, scoring for the prepared                   Heavy practice load; no GS overlap

 Graduation subject               Existing base and comfort                             Material and evaluation may be harder to
                                                                                        find
Source: Mentor guidance. No success-rate ranking is given because no official subject-wise success data is published by UPSC.

  Do not choose a subject because a coaching centre calls it 'scoring', or because a topper chose it. The
  evidence that matters is your own: read the syllabus, attempt a few past questions, and see whether the subject
  holds your attention for a month.

A step-by-step selection checklist
1 Download the official optional syllabus for your candidate subjects.

2 Shortlist three subjects that fit your background and interest.
3 Read each syllabus fully and mark topics you can and cannot handle.
4 Attempt one past paper per subject without preparation, timed.
5 Find the standard material and one evaluator for each finalist.
6 Commit to one subject and start with its basic reading.
7 Review after one month - if it is draining without progress, change now, not later.
keyTakeaways: Choose an optional by syllabus fit, interest, material access, writing comfort and realistic time.
No subject is universally best or guarantees marks.
Test the syllabus and past papers before committing.
nextAction: Compare two or three candidate optionals using the worksheet.
